text.default:
She has given you the one fact, east, and now she is waiting to see what you will do with it.

"When?" you ask.

"Fourteen months ago, or thereabouts." She looks at her hands. "They came to the camp after a week in Crestfall. They wanted to know about the ruins, what the camp knew and what I knew. I told them what I could."

She is quiet for a little.

"I should have told them more," she says, as much to herself as to you. "Or less. I am still not sure which."

She looks up. "What do you know about the ruins?"
text.commander:
"I know they're there," you say. "I know people go east and don't come back. And I know there are three lots of people in this town who each think they know what's in them, and they all think something different."

She very nearly smiles. "That is more than most people know when they arrive." She shifts on the log. "Your person was thorough. They asked the right questions. I gave them what I had, which was not everything, and they went east with it all the same."
text.arcane:
"Tell me what you know," you say.

She looks at you as though deciding how much your learning is worth. "What you know about the old workings would take a long time to trade," she says. "And I am not sure we use the same words for it."

"Try," you say.

She does. None of what she knows comes from books. She learned it by living beside the thing for three years, as you learn the weather.
text.ranger:
"East is Harrow. And past Harrow, the forest proper." She gives it as a direction, not a warning. "Your person went through Harrow and kept going. I know, because I was at the tree line that day." She stops. "I watched them go in."

You wait.

"They did not look afraid," she says. "That is what I keep coming back to. They looked as though they knew where they were going."
text.cipher:
She is telling you more than she meant to. You can see the moment she decides to; something in the set of her shoulders lets go.

"They were looking for the source," she says. "Not to stop it. To understand it." She pauses. "I told them that once they were past the tree line, there might not be much difference."

She looks you in the eye. "They went anyway."

choices.text: "What do you know about what's in the ruins?"

success.text:
She makes up her mind. "Come back tomorrow," she says. "There are things I can show you better than I can tell you. And I want to know more about who you are first."

It is a condition, not a refusal, and you accept it.

success_at_cost.text:
She gives you the outline. The ruins are old, older than any people the region has a record of. The power in them has been leaking out for three years, through the soil and the water. The camp has found ways to keep some of it off, though only some.

She does not tell you everything. What she keeps back, you suspect, is what she thinks is most dangerous.

failure.text: "I have told you what I can for today," Maret says, and that is the end of it. "Come back. Let me see a little more of who you are."

choices.text: Don't push any further. Stay and help with whatever the camp needs.

default.text: She looks at you as if she rather approves. "Branch can find you something useful to do," she says, and gets up. She has ended the conversation on her own terms, which means it can go on another time.

text.default:
She has shut up shop for the day, and you both know it. Whatever the name stirred in her, she has had time to put it away again, and she is not going to give you the opening you hoped for.

But she did not send you away. She said tomorrow. In a camp where Branch could have turned you round at the tree line, tomorrow is very nearly a welcome.

You get up. "Tomorrow, then."

"Tomorrow," she says. She watches you go. She has not made up her mind about you yet, and you leave her to do it.
text.commander:
You leave the camp knowing, as any soldier does, that a position you cannot take head on can usually be got round.

You will try again tomorrow, and try it differently, and find out more first. Frightened people shut tight, but they open again once they feel safe enough.
text.arcane: On the way out you take careful note of what you have seen: the herb garden especially, and the way the tents are laid out and the people placed among them. None of it is by chance. Maret has arranged the camp with a knowledge of what she is guarding against that goes a long way beyond instinct.
text.ranger: On the way out you take one more look at the camp: the ways out, how the watch is kept, the single path back through the trees to town. Maret chose the place carefully. It has good sight lines and more than one way out, and it can be defended without looking as though it could.
text.cipher:
You walk out of the camp with less than you wanted and a good deal more than nothing, which is not a bad first day.

Maret did not refuse you. She only put you off. People who keep putting you off generally get tired of it in the end.

choices.text: Stay at the edge of the camp and spend some time with the Rootless before you go.

default.text: You don't go straight away. You sit at the edge of the camp and let the place get used to you. After a while somebody sits down near you. It is Lira, a young woman, quiet, with the look of somebody the curse has partly taken.

choices.text: Go back to Crestfall, and come back tomorrow.

default.text: You walk back through the trees to Crestfall. The evening is coming on, grey and still.

text.default:
You spend the rest of the day at the camp, working alongside the Rootless. Branch finds you jobs: firewood, the herb garden, and checking the water for the cloudiness that Maret says means the curse has got into the source.

There are twenty-three of them, and you begin to know a few. There is an old farmer who says very little and watches everything, and two youngsters who are not of the same family but have decided to be. There is a woman who was a midwife in one of the villages to the east and now nurses people in the early stages of the curse.

Maret watches you work and tries not to let you see it. You let her.
text.commander:
You work. The camp is better organised than it looks from outside. Nobody gives orders, and the work goes to whoever can do it, so the whole place runs on people simply knowing what is wanted. Anyone brought up in a barracks would recognise it.

Branch finds you at the end of the day. "You know how to be useful without making a show of it," he says. You gather it is as near a compliment as he gets.
text.arcane:
The herb garden is much the most interesting thing in the camp. You work in it for an hour and identify fifteen different plants, three of which you have never come across in any book. The woman who planted it, a quiet old woman called Pol, watches you name them and says nothing at all until you get one wrong.

Then she corrects you, nods once, and goes back to her work.
text.ranger:
You work round the outside of the camp, checking the places Maret thinks are weak in whatever protection she has made. You find two that she missed, and you put them right without saying anything.

Branch sees you do it. He doesn't say anything either, but at supper he gives you a better piece of bread than anyone else's.
text.cipher:
You work and watch at the same time. By the end of the day you understand how the camp hangs together. Maret is at the centre of it, and Branch is her second and also the one who doubts her. Lira is the one the others look to without admitting it, and Pol knows more than anybody about what Maret is really doing.

You know now who holds the place up, and who listens to whom.

default.text: She is sitting at the edge of the camp working at a piece of rope. It is a knot you don't know.
He is sharpening a blade, slowly and with great care. He doesn't look up as you come over, but he doesn't tell you to go away.

success.text:
The well is a quarter of a mile back towards town, because the one in the camp tastes wrong. You carry two buckets each way, six times over. The midwife doesn't talk while she walks, and neither do you.

On the last trip she says, "The town well's the same depth as ours. It'll go the same way. Nobody there wants to hear it."

success_at_cost.text: You manage four trips before your shoulders give out. The midwife takes the last bucket from you without a word and carries it herself.

failure.text: On the second trip you slip on the bank by the well and go down hard, with the bucket on top of you. The midwife helps you up, looks at your wrist and tells you to sit down.

text.text: The light is going. Find Maret.
text.else: Wait for Maret to find you when the day's work is done.

default.text:
She comes to you when the evening fire is lit, sits down across it from you, and looks into it for a while.

"Tomorrow," she says, "I will tell you what I know. About your person, and about what I think is in those ruins." She pauses. "Tonight I want to ask you something first."

text.default:
She doesn't look up as you come over. She is working at the rope, and her hands seem to know what to do even when her head doesn't.

Lira is somewhere in her twenties. She was quick once, you think, the sort of girl who filled a room. She is careful now. The curse has not gone deep in her, but it is there. Every so often she is a moment late with a word, as though it had further to come than it should.

"The new one," she says, without looking up. "From outside. Maret said you're looking for someone."

"Yes," you say.

"Most people who come here are," she says. "Or they are by the end. Everyone's looking for someone."
text.commander:
You sit down near her and let the silence be. You have sat beside enough soldiers in field camps to know that sitting with somebody does not always mean talking.

"You're from outside," she says after a while. "Do you know what this looks like from outside?" She waves a hand at herself, and at the camp. "To people who haven't seen it?"
text.arcane:
You sit and watch her work the rope. The knot she is tying is one you have seen drawn in a book. It is a ward knot, older than the Covenant, of the kind used by the people who made the first seals.

"Where did you learn that?" you ask.

She looks up, and for a moment you can see the bright, quick girl she was, before the slowness comes back. "From the ruins," she says. "I was in the outskirts, before Maret found me."
text.ranger:
You crouch down near her, so that you are on her level, as you would with a nervous animal.

She seems to like it. "You move like you know where you are," she says. "Most people here stopped knowing where they are a while ago. Even before the curse."

She looks at the rope. "I was getting there. Then the curse came, and I stopped minding about before."
text.cipher:
You sit, and she works, and you watch her.

The slowness in her comes and goes. Some sentences she says at an ordinary pace, and in others the words arrive a second after they ought to. She is managing it, and has been for a while. Whatever Maret's methods can do to bring people back, Lira has gone as far with it as it goes.

choices.text: Ask her what the curse feels like from inside.

text: She takes a while to think how to answer. Then she tries.

"Like the volume being turned down," she says. "Not on sounds. On caring. Things stop mattering, but in the wrong order. Small things first, then middling things. I stopped minding whether I was hungry before I stopped minding whether I was safe, and that's the wrong way round."
You know the feeling she means. You left a town because of it.
"Maret's ways stopped it getting worse," she says. "I'm here. I'm mostly here. But I can feel the edge of where it stopped."
She holds up the rope. "The knot helps. Having something my hands know how to do. It keeps me from going thin."

success_at_cost.text: She tries to describe it, and runs out of words very quickly. "Like being cold, only it isn't the weather," she says. "And then getting used to the cold." She stops. "Maret helped me get less used to it."

failure.text:
She starts to try and loses the thread. After a moment she gives a small shake of the head and goes back to the rope.

"Sorry," she says. "Some days it's easier to say than others."

choices.text: Sit with her, and don't ask anything.

default.text:
You sit, and she works. After a while she shows you the knot. Your hands are clumsy at it, and she is patient with you without letting you see that she is being patient.

When they call everyone to the fire for supper, she looks at you.

"You did not ask me anything," she says. "That was good. Thank you."

text.default:
Branch goes on sharpening the blade without looking up. You sit down near him, and he goes on sharpening, and you wait.

After a couple of minutes he says, "You are going to ask me about the person you are looking for."

"I was going to wait until you'd finished the blade."

"The blade will be finished when I am satisfied with it, and that takes as long as it takes." He glances up. "Ask."

He has evidently decided long ago that saying what he means is the only way of talking worth the trouble. He isn't rude, and he means well, after his fashion. He simply won't pretend.
text.commander:
You know the type: a soldier who found that bowing and scraping took longer than saying what he meant. You talk to him the same way.

"You knew them," you say. "The person I'm looking for."

"I knew of them," says Branch. "They were in the camp three weeks. I do not get to know people in three weeks. I watch them."
text.arcane:
"You don't like me," you say.

He very nearly stops sharpening. "I do not trust you," he says. "That is a different thing. I do not like or dislike people I do not know. I make up my mind about them."

"And have you?"

"Not yet." He goes back to the blade. "Ask your question."
text.ranger:
You sit for a couple of minutes without speaking. Neither of you is troubled by it.

"Ranger," he says at last. "By the way you came through the trees."

"Soldier," you say. "By the way you stand."

He nods. It seems fair to him.
text.cipher:
Most of what works on other people will not work on him. He knows charm when he sees it, and authority, and he has decided neither has anything to do with him. You find that interesting rather than annoying.

You ask him straight out, since there is nothing else left to try, and since it happens to be true.

choices.text: "What did you see of the person I'm looking for?"

success.text:
He finishes the blade and puts it down.

"Capable," he says. "They asked the right questions, and they were not afraid of the answers, which is unusual." He looks at his hands. "They stayed longer than Maret expected. They did useful work. They helped with Lira." He stops. "Maret trusted them further than she usually trusts anyone so soon."

"And that worried you."

"Yes," he says. "Maret's judgement is good. Her judgement of the people she trusts quickly is not so good."

He has just told you something about Maret that she did not tell you herself.

success_at_cost.text: "Capable," he says. "They asked the right questions and they went east." He picks up the blade again. "That is what I know."

failure.text: "Maret can tell you what she wants to tell you," he says. "I do not speak for her." He goes back to his sharpening, and that is the end of it.

success.text:
He gives you a sharp look, and then decides to answer.

"Three years. I was in the third of the eastern villages when the curse began. She came through two weeks later and said she was looking for people who had not given up yet." He says it flatly, as though giving up would have been perfectly reasonable. "I had not. I went with her."

He is quiet a moment. "She saved my life three times in the first year. Nothing dramatic. She made the right decision at the right time, that is all." He looks at the blade. "I trust her judgement, except when I do not. That is the honest answer."

success_at_cost.text: "Long enough," he says. "Ask Maret, if you want her history. Mine is part of hers, so it is hers to tell."

failure.text: "Long enough," he says, and goes back to the blade. You will get no more out of him.

default.text:
He puts the blade down. "Third Eastern. Pikes." For the first time he looks at you as if you might be somebody he knows. "You were on a list. Casualties, the year of the river crossing. I read it in a tent I was not supposed to be in." He pauses. "You were not dead."

"No."

"Good," says Branch, and picks up the blade again.

default: The camp settles down for the evening and Maret comes to sit by the fire. She has made up her mind about you, not entirely, but far enough to go on.
She asks you something you were not expecting.
"Why did you leave?" she says. "Ashenveld. You were born here, and you left. Why?"
She is not asking out of politeness. The answer will tell her something she needs to know.

default.text: "Lira says you sat with her and asked nothing," Maret says. "That is rare."

text.commander:
"There was a war," you say. "And I was the sort of person who went to wars."

She nods. "And after the war?"

"After the war there was no good reason to come back. Until there was."
text.arcane:
"There's a library in the city," you say. "The biggest collection of pre-kingdom texts anywhere. I spent eleven years in it." You stop for a moment. "I thought I'd find more answers there than here."

"And did you?"

"I found different questions," you say. "Better put. It isn't the same thing."
text.ranger:
"The forest was getting smaller," you say. It is true, though you have never said it out loud before. "I knew everything here too well. I needed somewhere I didn't know the edges."

She looks at the trees. "And now the edges have come looking for you."
text.cipher:
You tell her something true, though not the whole truth, which is generally the way to get doors opened without giving much away.

"I left because someone made it possible," you say. "The same person I'm looking for. They made it easier to go than to stay, and then they disappeared, and now I'm back."

She is quiet for a moment. "You are grateful to them," she says, "and angry with them. That is a hard pair to carry."

choices.text: Answer honestly, and tell her all of it.

text: You tell her why you left. There was no reason you could point to. Crestfall was making you quiet, a little more every year, and one spring you got on a barge before it could finish the job.

text.text: And you tell her about [missing person]. You said you would write. You wrote twice.
And [missing person]. You left without telling them it was ending, so it never quite did.
And [missing person], two years younger, who you left with the house and your mother's last illness.
And [missing person], who told you to go. You thought they were tired of you. You never asked.
And [missing person]. You left after an argument neither of you finished. You have gone on having it, in your head, for eleven years.
And [missing person]. Nothing was ever said between you. You left before you had to say it.

text: She listens without interrupting, and without any show of listening.
When you have finished she is quiet for a while. "That is what it does to people here now," she says. "You felt it early."
Then she says, "I will tell you what I know tomorrow. All of it. What I know about the ruins, and what I know about your person."
She says it like somebody settling a debt. You have not asked what it will cost her.
It has cost you something to say it.

choices.text: Answer the part you're comfortable with.

bonus.label: You sat with Lira and asked nothing

success.text:
You tell her enough. She can see it is not everything, but it is enough for her to understand what kind of person would come back for the person you came back for.

She nods. "Tomorrow," she says. "I will tell you what I know."

success_at_cost.text: She takes what you give her and thinks about it. "Some of that is true," she says at last, quite mildly. "Come back tomorrow. I will tell you what I can tell someone I know this little about."

failure.text:
She hears you out and waits for more, and when no more comes she nods.

"I understand," she says. She means she understands why you are holding back, not that she is content with it. "Your person left a letter with me. I will keep it until I think you are the right person to have it."

default: The next morning Maret finds you before you can go looking for her. She has a letter.
It is not the letter that brought you here. It is another one, and shorter. [missing person] wrote it and left it with Maret two weeks before they went east.
Maret holds it out. You take it, and she watches your face while you read.

> I found it. It is real and it is below the ruins.
> I am going in. I may not come out. I know that.
> Do not follow me. Not until you know more than I did.
> [player].
Your name at the bottom is written as people write a name when it is the whole of what they want to say.
text.commander:
You read it twice. Years of discipline keep your face as you want it. Inside you are angry, as people are when a choice that was theirs has been made for them.

Maret is watching you closely. "They did not want you to come," she says. "They wanted you to know. But they did not want you to come."

"I know," you say. "I came anyway."

"I know," she says. "That is why I gave you the letter."
text.arcane:
The writing is theirs. You would know it anywhere.

What strikes you is that they found what they came for. They came looking for something in particular, and you never knew what. They knew a good deal more than they told you before they left.

"What did they know?" you ask Maret. "Before they went in."
text.ranger:
You stand up to read it. It seems wrong to sit down for it.

Every line is a plain fact, without any softening; that was always how they spoke to you. Not until you know more, it says.

You are here, and you know enough. You fold up the letter.
text.cipher:
Your face does nothing while you read. You were trained to keep it so.

Every line of it was meant for you. It was not written for whoever might find it, but for the one person who would be given it after they had gone into those ruins.

And at the end there is nothing but your name.

You fold the letter and keep your face exactly as it is.

choices.text: "What did they know when they went in? What did you tell them?"

default.text:
Maret tells you what she told them about the ruins: how far they go, what the camp found when it searched the outskirts, and where the deepest place is that anyone can reach. She told them what she understood of the source of the curse. And she told them about her arrangement with the forest.

Then she takes a folded paper from inside her coat and gives it to you. It is a list in her handwriting, numbered, thirty-eight lines long.

You read three of them. "My daughter's voice" is at the top. The name of the village is about halfway down. The last is "What I was going to say to Branch".

"Each new moon I walk to the tree line and give it one," she says. "It keeps the camp shallow, and the garden grows." She takes the list back. "I write them down so I know what I no longer have."

She told them everything she knew, and they went in all the same.

"I did not think they would go," she says. "I told myself I was giving them the facts so that they could choose for themselves. But the facts I gave them made the choice for them."

She looks at the trees. "Either I was wrong to send them in, or I was right, and they found something, and they are still there waiting for you. I do not know which."

choices.text: "I'm going east, whatever the letter says."

default.text:
She nods. "I know," she says. "That is why I gave you the letter. So that you would go in knowing what you were walking towards."

She tells you everything: the ruins, the source, the deepest place.

Then she takes a folded paper from inside her coat and gives it to you. It is a list in her handwriting, numbered, thirty-eight lines long.

You read three of them. "My daughter's voice" is at the top. The name of the village is about halfway down. The last is "What I was going to say to Branch".

"Each new moon I walk to the tree line and give it one," she says. "It keeps the camp shallow, and the garden grows." She takes the list back. "I write them down so I know what I no longer have."

She gives you all of it, just as she gave it to [missing person]. She has decided that not knowing is the greater danger.

default: She keeps the letter. She has told you it exists, and what you must do to have it, and that is a kindness of a sort. She need never have told you about it at all.

What she wants is not a small thing. She needs to know who you are. She is not interested in what you want or what you can do. She wants to know who you are, so that she knows what she would be giving it to.
You leave the camp that evening with no more than you came with, except that you now know there is a letter, and what it would take to be given it.

default.text: Before you go she shows you something else instead. It is a list in her handwriting, thirty-eight lines long, of the things she has given the forest to keep the camp safe. "My daughter's voice" is the first. "You have earned that much," she says.

text.commander:
You could try to push her. You think about it and decide not to. Pressure will not move Maret. Evidence might.

You go back the next day, and the day after. You work and you talk, and you let her see who you are by what you do rather than by what you say.
text.arcane:
You spend the next two days at the camp finding out what you can without the letter. Lira tells you about the outskirts of the ruins, and Branch about how the camp began, and the herb garden tells you a good deal about how much Maret knows.

It is a good deal, but it is not the letter.
text.ranger:
You spend two days going between the camp and the edge of the forest, looking at both. You watch how the curse moves, and which way it came from, and the place it seems to spread out from.

You have a fair idea where the source is before Maret tells you.
text.cipher: You spend the two days carefully. You spend them on Lira, who trusts freely once she has decided to, and on Branch, who is slow to trust anyone and then trusts them completely. Through the two of them you let the camp see who you are. On the second evening Maret comes to you.

choices.text: Come back, and show her who you are over the next two days.

success.text:
Two days later she gives you the letter.

She does not say what has changed. She simply hands it to you by the fire one morning and sits across from you while you read it. She looks like somebody keeping a promise she was not sure she would be able to keep.

success_at_cost.text:
She tells you what she knows: what she told [missing person], where they went, and what she thinks is in the ruins. But she keeps the letter.

"The letter is theirs to give," she says. "Not mine. If you find them, they can give it to you themselves."

She pauses. "I hope you find them," she says, and she means it.

failure.text:
She doesn't give you the letter. She tells you enough to go east, the way and the distance and where the ruins are, but she keeps it.

"I am sorry," she says. "I know it is not what you wanted."

You go east without it.

choices.text: Leave it, and go back to town.

default.text: You don't go back. Maret doesn't send for you. On the third morning you hear that she has been asking Branch whether you have left yet.
